topic.title: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change
topic.summary: Polynomial vocabulary, local and global extrema, how zeros and turning points relate, and inflection points.

lesson.title: Polynomial Functions and Rates of Change
lesson.summary: Polynomial vocabulary, local and global extrema, how zeros and turning points relate, and inflection points.
learningGoals: Name the degree, leading term, and leading coefficient of a polynomial.
Distinguish local from global maxima and minima and explain where they occur.
Use the sign pattern of rates of change to locate extrema and inflection points.
lesson.bigIdea: A polynomial's graph is shaped by how its rate of change rises and falls. Extrema mark where it changes direction, and inflection points mark where it changes concavity.
lesson.context: You have studied how outputs change and how rates themselves change. Polynomial functions are the first large family where both ideas appear in rich combination, and they are built from the simple power functions you already know.

sections.title: A polynomial function is a sum of terms with whole-number powers.

blocks.text: A nonconstant polynomial function is equivalent to a sum of terms, each a real number times a power of x, where every power is a positive whole number or zero. Written in order, it looks like aₙxⁿ + aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ + … + a₁x + a₀, with aₙ ≠ 0. The exponent n is the degree, aₙxⁿ is the leading term, and aₙ is the leading coefficient.

A product of factors still counts as a polynomial, because it is equivalent to a sum of powers once expanded. Rules such as 5/x or √x are not polynomials, since x appears in a denominator or under a radical instead of with a whole-number power.

sections.takeaway: Degree comes from the highest power of x after the polynomial is fully expanded.

sections.title: Extrema occur where a function switches between increasing and decreasing.

blocks.text: A local maximum occurs where a function switches from increasing to decreasing, and a local minimum occurs where it switches from decreasing to increasing. A local extremum can also occur at an included endpoint of the domain. A local extremum whose output beats every other output of the function is a global maximum or a global minimum.

The outputs rise from −2 to 2 as x goes from −2 to −1, then fall to −2 at x = 1, then rise again. So f has a local maximum near x = −1 and a local minimum near x = 1. Neither is global: the outputs of a cubic keep growing without bound in one direction and shrinking in the other.

blocks.title: Even-degree polynomials
blocks.text: An even-degree polynomial always has a global maximum or a global minimum, because both ends of its graph turn the same way. For a quadratic, that extreme output occurs at the vertex.

sections.takeaway: A local extremum is the best output nearby. A global extremum is the best output everywhere.

sections.title: Between two real zeros, a polynomial must turn around.

blocks.text: If a polynomial has two different real zeros, its output is 0 at both. To leave 0 and later return to 0, the function must change direction somewhere in between. So there is at least one local maximum or minimum between any two distinct real zeros.

Consider f(x) = x(x − 2)(x + 2) = x³ − 4x, which has zeros at −2, 0, and 2. Between −2 and 0 the graph rises above the x-axis and turns around, giving a local maximum of about 3.08 near x = −1.15. Between 0 and 2 the graph dips below the axis, giving a local minimum of about −3.08 near x = 1.15.

sections.takeaway: At least one turning point sits between any two distinct real zeros of a polynomial.

sections.title: Inflection points are where concavity changes.

blocks.text: An inflection point is where the rate of change switches between increasing and decreasing, so the graph switches between concave up and concave down. Extrema describe direction. Inflection points describe curvature, and they are different features that can occur at different inputs.

blocks.caption: Values and changes of f(x) = x³

blocks.text: The output changes drop from 7 to 1 on the left, then climb from 1 to 7 on the right. The rate of change is decreasing before x = 0 and increasing after it, so the graph is concave down to the left of 0 and concave up to the right. The inflection point is at x = 0.

sections.takeaway: At an inflection point the graph changes concavity. At an extremum the graph changes direction.

vocabulary.definition: A function equivalent to a sum of terms of the form a·xⁿ, where each a is a real number and each n is zero or a positive whole number.
The highest power of x in a polynomial after it is fully expanded.
The term of a polynomial with the highest power of x.
The coefficient of the leading term of a polynomial.
An output at an input where a function switches from increasing to decreasing, or at an included endpoint where it is greater than nearby outputs.
An output at an input where a function switches from decreasing to increasing, or at an included endpoint where it is less than nearby outputs.
A local maximum whose output is greater than every other output of the function.
A local minimum whose output is less than every other output of the function.
A point where the rate of change switches between increasing and decreasing, so the concavity of the graph changes.

connections.title: Quadratics are the simplest case
connections.body: A quadratic has one vertex, which is a global extremum, and no inflection point because its rates change at a constant pace. Higher-degree polynomials can have several extrema and inflection points.
connections.transferQuestion: Why can a quadratic never have an inflection point?
connections.feedback: Its average rates change by a constant amount in one direction, so the graph never switches between concave up and concave down.

connections.title: Zeros and end behavior finish the picture
connections.body: Topic 1.5 will connect real zeros to factors and to where the graph crosses or touches the x-axis. Topic 1.6 will use the leading term to describe where the graph goes at the far left and far right.
connections.transferQuestion: What two kinds of information about a polynomial graph would you want in order to sketch it?
connections.feedback: A strong answer includes the zeros and the end behavior, and then adds turning points and concavity to refine the shape.

glossary.definition: A graph is concave up where its rate of change is increasing.
A graph is concave down where its rate of change is decreasing.
A function that can be written ax² + bx + c with a ≠ 0. Its average rates over consecutive equal-width intervals form a linear pattern.
